turns.prompt: A company keeps a single table employees(emp_id, name, dept_name, dept_floor), with the department's floor repeated on every employee row. What goes wrong when the Sales department moves to another floor, when you want to record a new department that has no employees yet, and when the last employee of a department leaves? How would you fix the design?
turns.answer: The current design suffers from an update anomaly (changing the Sales floor requires updating every Sales employee row, risking inconsistent floors), an insertion anomaly (you can’t record a new department until it has at least one employee) and a deletion anomaly (removing the last employee also removes the only record of that department’s floor). The fix is to normalize by creating a separate departments table (dept_id, dept_name, dept_floor) and store only dept_id as a foreign key in employees.

turns.prompt: A teammate needs to check whether a customer ID is in an unsorted Python list of one million IDs. They say: "`if cid in ids:` is O(1) because it is a single line, so it beats any loop I could write; and if it ever got slow, I would just run binary search on the list instead." What is wrong with each of these two claims?
turns.answer: `cid in ids` does a linear scan of the list, so its time is O(n) (just like an explicit loop, only a bit faster because the loop runs in C). Binary search only works on sorted data; on an unsorted list it could discard the half that actually contains the ID and give a false‑negative, so you’d need to sort first (or use a set) for fast membership checks.
